title: LLM Inference Challenges: Memory, Fragmentation, Duplicate Work
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: In Part 1, we understood how KV caching makes generation fast by avoiding repeated computation.
A natural next question is:
If KV caching improves speed, what problems does it introduce?
At a high level, four issues show up:

Memory explosion
Fragmentation
Duplicate computation
Low GPU utilization (we’ll cover this and large model overhead in the next part)
Let’s go step by step and build intuition the same way.
Memory Explosion
If KV caching avoids recomputation, it does so by storing everything.
For every token and every layer (and in practice, for every attention head), key and value vectors are stored. As tokens grow, memory grows.
This leads to the first real problem: memory explosion.
How do we fix memory explosion?
Three common approaches are used:

Paged attention
Quantization
Offloading
Let’s go one by one.
Paged Attention (Blocks)
To really understand why paged attention is needed, it helps to walk through a slightly more detailed example.
Without Blocks (Continuous Memory Requirement)
Assume GPU memory is arranged like this (each box is a unit of memory):

User A uses 3 units
User B uses 3 units
User C uses 3 units
Now suppose User B finishes:
We now have free memory, but it is split into two parts:

3 units in the middle
1 unit at the end
Now a new request (User D) arrives and needs 4 units.
Even though we have 4 units total, they are not continuous:
So User D cannot be allocated.
This is fragmentation.
With Blocks (Paged Attention)
Now instead of requiring one continuous chunk, we divide memory into fixed-size blocks.
Each request is allowed to use multiple blocks, even if they are not next to each other.
Let’s reuse the same scenario.
After User B finishes:
Now User D needs 4 blocks.
With paged attention, we can allocate any 4 free blocks, even if they are scattered:
Here, User D is using:

3 blocks from the middle
1 block from the end
But how does the model know the order?
This is the key idea.
Even though blocks are scattered physically, the system keeps a mapping like:
User D → Block 4, Block 5, Block 6, Block 10
This mapping is stored in something like a block table.
So when the model reads the sequence, it follows the logical order, not the physical layout.
Why this fixes the problem

We no longer require continuous memory
Any free block can be reused
Memory gaps no longer cause allocation failures
This makes memory usage much more efficient and scalable.

Offloading
If memory is still not enough, part of the KV cache can be moved out of GPU memory.
Typically:

GPU memory → fast but limited
CPU memory → slower but much larger
So active data stays on GPU, and less active data moves to CPU.
Downsides of Offloading
Offloading is useful, but it is not ideal in all cases.

Data transfer between CPU and GPU is slow
If data is needed frequently, performance drops
Real-time systems may not tolerate this latency
So offloading is best when:

data is not accessed frequently
memory is the main bottleneck
Fragmentation
Even if total memory is sufficient, allocation can still fail because memory is not arranged properly.
Example:
This is fragmentation—memory exists, but not in the shape required.
Paged attention solves this as well.
Since memory is divided into blocks, requests no longer require continuous space. Blocks can be reused and placed anywhere.
How does the GPU know where blocks are?
The system uses a mapping table (often called a block table).
This table maps:
logical token positions → physical memory blocks
So even if blocks are scattered, the model reads them as if they were continuous.
Duplicate Computation
KV caching works well within a single request, but across requests, the same work can still be repeated.
Example:
User 1: "Answer clearly: What is AI?" User 2: "Answer clearly: What is ML?"
Both share the prefix:
"Answer clearly:"
Without optimization:

the prefix is computed twice
KV cache is duplicated
Prefix Caching
Prefix caching reuses KV cache for identical prefixes across requests. Instead of recomputing the shared prefix:

compute it once
reuse it for other requests with the same prefix
This reduces computation, improves time to first token, and avoids duplicating memory.
More detailed examples
1) Simple shared prefix
User 1: "Explain transformers in simple terms" User 2: "Explain transformers with examples"
Shared prefix: "Explain transformers"

Without prefix caching: the prefix is computed twice and stored twice.
With prefix caching: compute the prefix once, reuse it, and only compute the differing suffixes.
2) System prompt (very common)
"You are a helpful assistant. Answer clearly and concisely."

Without prefix caching: recompute this for every request.
With prefix caching: compute once and reuse across users.
3) Retrieval (RAG) with large context
"Answer based on this document: "
User 1: "... What is section 1?" User 2: "... What is section 2?"

Without prefix caching: process the entire document for each request.
With prefix caching: process once and reuse KV cache for all follow-ups.
4) Repeated templates or workflows
"Summarize the following text:" or repeated agent instructions.

Without prefix caching: template is recomputed each time.
With prefix caching: template KV cache is reused.
Important nuance
Prefix caching only works when the prefix matches exactly at the token level. Small differences can prevent reuse.
Conceptually, this is similar to reusing a template instead of recreating it each time.
What Comes Next
At this point, we have handled:

memory explosion
fragmentation
duplicate computation
Two important problems remain:

low GPU utilization
large model overhead
We will cover both in the next part.
